blocks.text: Dohra:

(After the narration of Banda Singh's execution) David Murray asked the author, That the author should also narrate (the post Banda Singh situation). After getting Banda Singh executed by (the Mughals), Where did the Khalsa Singhs stay and survive? (1)
lines: (After the narration of Banda Singh's execution) David Murray asked the author,
That the author should also narrate (the post Banda Singh situation).
After getting Banda Singh executed by (the Mughals),
Where did the Khalsa Singhs stay and survive?

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Then, I (the author) explained to David Murray, That Khalsa Singhs stayed and survived in the same country (Punjab). As all species of birds stay and survive among falcons, Or the way the deer find shelter in the midst of lions' dens. (2)
lines: Then,
I (the author) explained to David Murray,
That Khalsa Singhs stayed and survived in the same country (Punjab).
As all species of birds stay and survive among falcons,
Or the way the deer find shelter in the midst of lions' dens.

blocks.text: While some Singhs picked up jobs and some got awards of landed property, Others settled down in religious places and Khalsa settlements. While some Singhs got exemption from payment of land revenue, Many others succumbed to the various temptations of the Mughals. (3)
lines: While some Singhs picked up jobs and some got awards of landed property,
Others settled down in religious places and Khalsa settlements.
While some Singhs got exemption from payment of land revenue,
Many others succumbed to the various temptations of the Mughals.

blocks.text: Dohra:

However, those among the Singhs owing allegiance to the Tat Khalsa1 , Did not succumb to any kind of temptations of the Mughals. Bearing every kind of scarcity, hunger and tribulations, They did not hesitate to the make any kind of sacrifice. (4)
lines: However, those among the Singhs owing allegiance to the Tat Khalsa1 ,
Did not succumb to any kind of temptations of the Mughals.
Bearing every kind of scarcity, hunger and tribulations,
They did not hesitate to the make any kind of sacrifice.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

They, being genuine Khalsa Singhs and as brave -hearted as lions, Cound not be subdued and overpowered by the Mughals. Taking refuge in the wild bushes, ferns and forests, They survived through loot and plunder of the Mughals. (5)
lines: They, being genuine Khalsa Singhs and as brave -hearted as lions,
Cound not be subdued and overpowered by the Mughals.
Taking refuge in the wild bushes, ferns and forests,
They survived through loot and plunder of the Mughals.

blocks.text: They would neither allow a safe passage to the Mughal caravans, Nor would they stay permanently at one place. Those alone are entitled to call themselves Tat Khalsa, Who have no fear of being killed or fighting a war. (6)
lines: They would neither allow a safe passage to the Mughal caravans,
Nor would they stay permanently at one place.
Those alone are entitled to call themselves Tat Khalsa,
Who have no fear of being killed or fighting a war.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Some of the Bandhayee Singhs had somehow survived, By hiding themselves from the prying eyes of the Mughals. Those among these who found favour with the (Tat) Khalsa, Were taken back and accepted into Khalsa fold. (7)
lines: Some of the Bandhayee Singhs had somehow survived,
By hiding themselves from the prying eyes of the Mughals.
Those among these who found favour with the (Tat) Khalsa,
Were taken back and accepted into Khalsa fold.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

But these Bandhayee Singhs nursed a secret grudge, And always wanted to keep their own distinct identity. They always wished to strengthen their own cadres, And kept on brewing hostility against the Singhs. (8)
lines: But these Bandhayee Singhs nursed a secret grudge,
And always wanted to keep their own distinct identity.
They always wished to strengthen their own cadres,
And kept on brewing hostility against the Singhs.

blocks.text: The factional Fight Between (Tat Khalsa) Singhs And Bandhayee Singhs (Tat Khalsa) Singhs decided thus....)
Dohra:
The way there occured a fierce rioting, Between the (Tat Khalsa) Singhs and the Bandhayee Singhs, And the way they plundered and killed each other, I would now narrate those circumstances. (1)
lines: The way there occured a fierce rioting,
Between the (Tat Khalsa) Singhs and the Bandhayee Singhs,
And the way they plundered and killed each other,
I would now narrate those circumstances.

blocks.text: Chaupai After disengaging his contingents from Bandhayee Singhs, Kahan Singh entered into agreement with the Mughals.
Settling for a daily receipt of five hundred rupees from the Mughals, He could also keep a contingent of five hundred horse-mounted troops. (2)
lines: Settling for a daily receipt of five hundred rupees from the Mughals,
He could also keep a contingent of five hundred horse-mounted troops.

blocks.text: Donning the blue (Khalsa) robes and steel rings (round his turban), He followed the initiated Singhs' code of conduct. Reciting the Sikh scriptures and making prayers everyday, He did not shirk from fighting and rioting (against his enemies). (3)
lines: Donning the blue (Khalsa) robes and steel rings (round his turban),
He followed the initiated Singhs' code of conduct.
Reciting the Sikh scriptures and making prayers everyday,
He did not shirk from fighting and rioting (against his enemies).

blocks.text: Keeping the Muslim Muezzins and butchers (of cows) at bay, He would put up his camp away from the Mughal troops. Settling for establishing his contingents camp at Amritsar, He also decided to hold an (annual) Khalsa congregation there. (4)
lines: Keeping the Muslim Muezzins and butchers (of cows) at bay,
He would put up his camp away from the Mughal troops.
Settling for establishing his contingents camp at Amritsar,
He also decided to hold an (annual) Khalsa congregation there.

blocks.text: Whatever amount the Singhs would be receiving as offerings, They would pay a part of this as tax to the Mughals. As the time for holding the annual congregation drew near, Baba Kahan Singh despatched a letter of invitation to the Sikh congregations. (5)
lines: Whatever amount the Singhs would be receiving as offerings,
They would pay a part of this as tax to the Mughals.
As the time for holding the annual congregation drew near,
Baba Kahan Singh despatched a letter of invitation to the Sikh congregations.

blocks.text: Informing the Sikhs about his agreement with the Mughal rulers, He exhorted the Sikhs to visit Amritsar without any fear. After receiving these invitations, the Sikhs from Lahore, Peshawar and Delhi, As well as from all other directions marched towards Amritsar. (6)
lines: Informing the Sikhs about his agreement with the Mughal rulers,
He exhorted the Sikhs to visit Amritsar without any fear.
After receiving these invitations, the Sikhs from Lahore,
Peshawar and Delhi,
As well as from all other directions marched towards Amritsar.

blocks.text: Dohra:

It became widely known (among the Sikhs), That the Mughals had been compelled to enter into a treaty. Since the Mughals had entered into agreement with vows on the holy Koran, The Sikhs did not need to have any apprehensions on this count. (7)
lines: It became widely known (among the Sikhs),
That the Mughals had been compelled to enter into a treaty.
Since the Mughals had entered into agreement with vows on the holy Koran,
The Sikhs did not need to have any apprehensions on this count.

blocks.text: After entering into a deal (to keep peace and harmony), Both the Singhs and the Mughals vowed to abide by the deal. Thereafter, the Mughal rulers sent written orders throughout the country, That the Mughal officials should provide security to the Sikh pilgrims. (8)
lines: After entering into a deal (to keep peace and harmony),
Both the Singhs and the Mughals vowed to abide by the deal.
Thereafter, the Mughal rulers sent written orders throughout the country,
That the Mughal officials should provide security to the Sikh pilgrims.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The Mughal rulers directed all their police officials, That no body should commit violence on the marching Sikh pilgrims, The police must provide complete security during pilgrimage, And ensure that the Sikh pilgrims reached Amritsar safely. (9)
lines: The Mughal rulers directed all their police officials,
That no body should commit violence on the marching Sikh pilgrims,
The police must provide complete security during pilgrimage,
And ensure that the Sikh pilgrims reached Amritsar safely.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Ten thousand in gold coins were settled to be collected as tax, Out of the total offerings made at the (Amritsar) congregation. The congregation's duration was settled to be for ten days, And the security cover would continue for that period. (10)
lines: Ten thousand in gold coins were settled to be collected as tax,
Out of the total offerings made at the (Amritsar) congregation.
The congregation's duration was settled to be for ten days,
And the security cover would continue for that period.

blocks.text: Sortha:

Having taken a firm decision (after hearing these assurances), The Sikhs had no doubts about their safety (during pilgrimage). Even if they died during this pilgrimage to the Guru's shrine, It would be a death better than their worldly existence. (11)
lines: Having taken a firm decision (after hearing these assurances),
The Sikhs had no doubts about their safety (during pilgrimage).
Even if they died during this pilgrimage to the Guru's shrine,
It would be a death better than their worldly existence.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Then a large number of Sikh pilgrims arrived at the congregation, And offerings amounted to a huge sum in money terms. Since the offerings touched a very high figure in money terms, The Singhs took possession of it after paying the settled tax to the Mughals. (12)
lines: Then a large number of Sikh pilgrims arrived at the congregation,
And offerings amounted to a huge sum in money terms.
Since the offerings touched a very high figure in money terms,
The Singhs took possession of it after paying the settled tax to the Mughals.

blocks.text: Bandhayee Singhs, feeling envious of (such a huge offering), They started laying claims to their share in these offerings. Khalsa Singhs told (Bandhayee Singhs) that they had no basis for such a claim, Since there was no ideological similarity between the two factions. (13)
lines: Bandhayee Singhs, feeling envious of (such a huge offering),
They started laying claims to their share in these offerings.
Khalsa Singhs told (Bandhayee Singhs) that they had no basis for such a claim,
Since there was no ideological similarity between the two factions.

blocks.text: They declared "Fateh Darshan" against Khalsa's "Waheguru ji ki Fateh3", They were Bishnois4 against Khalsa's casteless fraternity. They donned red robes against Khalsa's rejection of such robes, The Khalsa donned blue robes against their dislike of blue robes. (14)
lines: They declared "Fateh Darshan" against Khalsa's "Waheguru ji ki Fateh3",
They were Bishnois4 against Khalsa's casteless fraternity.
They donned red robes against Khalsa's rejection of such robes,
The Khalsa donned blue robes against their dislike of blue robes.

blocks.text: The holy shrine at Amritsar never belonged to Bandhayee Singhs, As they never had any share in the offerings at this shrine. The Bandhayee Singhs had great misconception about their following, That all the Sikhs would become followers of Banda Singh's religion. (15)
lines: The holy shrine at Amritsar never belonged to Bandhayee Singhs,
As they never had any share in the offerings at this shrine.
The Bandhayee Singhs had great misconception about their following,
That all the Sikhs would become followers of Banda Singh's religion.

blocks.text: They claimed that after the (Tenth) Guru had vested his power in Banda Singh, The whole Sodhi dynasty (of Sikh Gurus) would stand discredited. Being nitwits they neither understood how the Khalsa Panth was raised, Nor the fact that the Guru had vested all his powers in the Khalsa Panth. (16)
lines: They claimed that after the (Tenth) Guru had vested his power in Banda Singh,
The whole Sodhi dynasty (of Sikh Gurus) would stand discredited.
Being nitwits they neither understood how the Khalsa Panth was raised,
Nor the fact that the Guru had vested all his powers in the Khalsa Panth.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Failing to get any share in the offerings at this time, The Bandhayee Singhs thought of claiming their share at the next (annual) congregation. Having decided to fight it out for claiming their share, They put up their camp in one corner of the (Amritsar) shrine. (17)
lines: Failing to get any share in the offerings at this time,
The Bandhayee Singhs thought of claiming their share at the next (annual) congregation.
Having decided to fight it out for claiming their share,
They put up their camp in one corner of the (Amritsar) shrine.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

These Bandhayee Singhs, with the view of establishing their camp, Fenced a sizeable area in the vicinity of Sikh Bungas5 and Sikh standards. They occupied this territory through fencing and digging a deep channel, In the space adjacent to the main entrance (to the shrine). (18)
lines: These Bandhayee Singhs, with the view of establishing their camp,
Fenced a sizeable area in the vicinity of Sikh Bungas5 and Sikh standards.
They occupied this territory through fencing and digging a deep channel,
In the space adjacent to the main entrance (to the shrine).

blocks.text: By putting up so many thatched cottages and makeshift shelters, The Bandhayee Singhs occupied this portion through use of force. After putting up their camp in that occupied portion, They kept on increasing their followers among their ranks. (19)
lines: By putting up so many thatched cottages and makeshift shelters,
The Bandhayee Singhs occupied this portion through use of force.
After putting up their camp in that occupied portion,
They kept on increasing their followers among their ranks.

blocks.text: With the continuous display of miracles learnt from Banda Singh, They kept on raising the strength of their followers. Since majority of the people become Sikhs for serving their vested interests, And adopt a Guru who serves their worldly needs best. (20)
lines: With the continuous display of miracles learnt from Banda Singh,
They kept on raising the strength of their followers.
Since majority of the people become Sikhs for serving their vested interests,
And adopt a Guru who serves their worldly needs best.

blocks.text: With this manifold increase in the ranks of Bandhayee Singhs, They felt extremely arrogant and defiant about their power. They declared that they would hold a separate congregation, And collect their offerings separately (from the main shrine). (21)
lines: With this manifold increase in the ranks of Bandhayee Singhs,
They felt extremely arrogant and defiant about their power.
They declared that they would hold a separate congregation,
And collect their offerings separately (from the main shrine).

blocks.text: Dohra:

At this, the (Tat Kahsa) Singhs reached a conclusion, That the Bandhayee Singhs were bent upon rioting. Either the Khalsa Singhs should destroy them through fighting, Or they should accept the latter's supremacy passively. (22)
lines: At this, the (Tat Kahsa) Singhs reached a conclusion,
That the Bandhayee Singhs were bent upon rioting.
Either the Khalsa Singhs should destroy them through fighting,
Or they should accept the latter's supremacy passively.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

As the wise amog the Singhs tried to advise patience to the hawks, The fiery Nihang Singhs declared their determination to fight it out. Why should they postpone their show of strength against the Bandhayees, When the Singhs had the nerve to fight against the mighty Mughals. (23)
lines: As the wise amog the Singhs tried to advise patience to the hawks,
The fiery Nihang Singhs declared their determination to fight it out.
Why should they postpone their show of strength against the Bandhayees,
When the Singhs had the nerve to fight against the mighty Mughals.

blocks.text: They would be setting a wrong precedent by sharing offerings with the Bandhayees, As this sharing of Gurdwara offerings would be an act of impropriety. They would never allow a wrong precedent to be set up, Even if it involved fighting and shedding their blood for it. (24)
lines: They would be setting a wrong precedent by sharing offerings with the Bandhayees,
As this sharing of Gurdwara offerings would be an act of impropriety.
They would never allow a wrong precedent to be set up,
Even if it involved fighting and shedding their blood for it.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Then those mature and cool-headed among them advised, That the Nihang Singhs should keep patience for the time-being. Let the Sikh pilgrims who had come for annual congregation depart, Then they were free to fight it out with the Bandhayee Singhs. (25)
lines: Then those mature and cool-headed among them advised,
That the Nihang Singhs should keep patience for the time-being.
Let the Sikh pilgrims who had come for annual congregation depart,
Then they were free to fight it out with the Bandhayee Singhs.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

So the Khalsa Singhs pleaded with the Bandhayee Singhs, That it was improper for them to strife against each other. In case they indulged in an internecine war among themselves, The Mughals would intervene and harm the innocent Sikh pilgrims. (26)
lines: So the Khalsa Singhs pleaded with the Bandhayee Singhs,
That it was improper for them to strife against each other.
In case they indulged in an internecine war among themselves,
The Mughals would intervene and harm the innocent Sikh pilgrims.

blocks.text: Dohra:

As two rival sparrows get entangled with each other, A (wily) cat quietly devours both these entangled sparrows. Similarly, the Mughals finding them entangled with each other, Would pounce upon them (like that wily cat). (27)
lines: As two rival sparrows get entangled with each other,
A (wily) cat quietly devours both these entangled sparrows.
Similarly, the Mughals finding them entangled with each other,
Would pounce upon them (like that wily cat).

blocks.text: Chaupai:

As the Bandhayee Singhs heard this persuasive tone of the Singhs, They felt all the more arrogant (about their power). As the Singhs had approached them subdued and humbled, They must be got thrashed at the hands of the Mughals. (28)
lines: As the Bandhayee Singhs heard this persuasive tone of the Singhs,
They felt all the more arrogant (about their power).
As the Singhs had approached them subdued and humbled,
They must be got thrashed at the hands of the Mughals.

blocks.text: By offering to pay double the amount of taxation to the Mughals, The Bandhayee Singhs planned to get the Singhs beaten by the Mughals. The Mughals, being always greedy of amassing wealth, Would definitely punish the Singhs for a consideration. (29)
lines: By offering to pay double the amount of taxation to the Mughals,
The Bandhayee Singhs planned to get the Singhs beaten by the Mughals.
The Mughals, being always greedy of amassing wealth,
Would definitely punish the Singhs for a consideration.

blocks.text: Dohra:

So, the Bandhayee Singhs immediately sent a despach to the Mughals, Throwing the bait of paying a larger amount of taxation. The Bandhayee Singhs would pay double the amount of taxation, In case, the Mughals made the Bandhayees partners in the shrine offerings. (30)
lines: So, the Bandhayee Singhs immediately sent a despach to the Mughals,
Throwing the bait of paying a larger amount of taxation.
The Bandhayee Singhs would pay double the amount of taxation,
In case, the Mughals made the Bandhayees partners in the shrine offerings.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The Mughals were always on the lookout for such an opportunity, Whereby they could get both greater revenue and decimation of Singhs. This (two pronged) strategy attracted the Mughal officials most, Whereby the Singhs got entangled with each other and got killed. (31)
lines: The Mughals were always on the lookout for such an opportunity,
Whereby they could get both greater revenue and decimation of Singhs.
This (two pronged) strategy attracted the Mughal officials most,
Whereby the Singhs got entangled with each other and got killed.

blocks.text: That the Bandhayee Singhs were bent upon shedding blood, The Singhs became absolutely clear about their intentions. That the Bandhayee Singhs would never stop bothering them, Without a straight fight with the Bandhayee Singhs. (32)
lines: That the Bandhayee Singhs were bent upon shedding blood,
The Singhs became absolutely clear about their intentions.
That the Bandhayee Singhs would never stop bothering them,
Without a straight fight with the Bandhayee Singhs.

blocks.text: Dohra:

So the (Nihang) Singhs arrived at a firm resolution, To fight it out irrespective of the consequences of their act. They must put the Bandhayee Singhs to sword, As well as the Mughals along with the Bandhayee Singhs. (33)
lines: So the (Nihang) Singhs arrived at a firm resolution,
To fight it out irrespective of the consequences of their act.
They must put the Bandhayee Singhs to sword,
As well as the Mughals along with the Bandhayee Singhs.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

(Baba) Kahan Singh pleaded with the Singhs once again, That violence at that moment would damage their reputation. Since they had invited the Sikh pilgrims from distant places, It would be improper if they got killed in such a violence. (34)
lines: (Baba) Kahan Singh pleaded with the Singhs once again,
That violence at that moment would damage their reputation.
Since they had invited the Sikh pilgrims from distant places,
It would be improper if they got killed in such a violence.

blocks.text: He advised the Singhs to bear all provocations with patience, And desist from indulging in violence during the congregation. Once the pilgrims departed for their homes after the congregation, The Singhs were free to take any action whatsoever they liked. (35)
lines: He advised the Singhs to bear all provocations with patience,
And desist from indulging in violence during the congregation.
Once the pilgrims departed for their homes after the congregation,
The Singhs were free to take any action whatsoever they liked.
